seo.title: 27 Best Consulting Logos Explained by a Brand Designer [2026]
seo.description: 27 consulting firm logos explained by a brand designer: McKinsey, BCG and Bain, the Big Four, Accenture and other large firms, plus specialist consultancies like ZS, Slalom and Korn Ferry.

intro:
The best consulting logos are clean wordmarks with one memorable detail. Most firms sell expertise, not a product, so their logos lead with the name and signal clarity, confidence and scale. The ones you remember add a single ownable element: BCG's green square, Deloitte's green dot, Accenture's purple arrow or EY's yellow beam.

What makes a good consulting logo?

The name comes first: clients hire a firm's reputation, so most consulting logos are wordmarks. Many firms shorten long names to initials, like BCG, EY, KPMG, PwC and ZS.

One distinctive detail: a colour, a dot, a beam or a symbol does more for recognition than a complicated icon.

A tone that fits the client: strategy firms look like private banks, technology consultancies look like software brands, and specialist firms often use a symbol that hints at their focus.

Below are 27 consulting logos in three groups: strategy consulting firms, the Big Four and large firms, and specialist and boutique consultancies. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. If you run a consultancy, also read my guide to consultancy branding, and see my law firm logos, investment firm logos and bank logos.

logoResearch.name: McKinsey & Company
logoResearch.verifiedFact: James O. McKinsey founded the firm in Chicago in 1926.
observations: A refined serif sets the name over two lines, with "& Company" indented under McKinsey.
Dark navy and old-style letters make the brand feel like a private bank or a law firm.

logoResearch.name: Boston Consulting Group
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bruce Henderson founded BCG in Boston in 1963.
observations: Three white letters sit in a solid green square, so the firm is known by its initials.
Green is rare among strategy firms and makes the mark easy to spot on a crowded page.

logoResearch.name: Bain & Company
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bill Bain and other former BCG consultants founded Bain & Company in Boston in 1973.
observations: Widely spaced red capitals spell out the full name with an ampersand.
A small circle with a pointer at the end works as a compact symbol for social icons.

logoResearch.name: Oliver Wyman
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Oliver Wyman was founded in New York in 1984 and is now part of Marsh McLennan.
observations: Heavy, wide capitals make the two names look solid and modern.
The line "A Marsh Business" under the name shows the parent company inside the logo.

logoResearch.name: Kearney
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kearney traces its history to 1926 and shortened its name from A.T. Kearney in 2020.
observations: Thin, very widely spaced capitals make the name feel calm and precise.
For its centenary the logo adds a 100 in a pink-to-purple gradient, the only colour in the mark.

logoResearch.name: Roland Berger
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Roland Berger founded the firm in Munich in 1967, and it is one of Europe's largest strategy consultancies.
observations: The founder's name is stacked over two lines in a rounded geometric sans serif.
With no symbol and no colour, the logo relies entirely on the shape of the letters.

logoResearch.name: L.E.K. Consulting
logoResearch.verifiedFact: L.E.K. Consulting was founded in London in 1983 by Jim Lawrence, Iain Evans and Richard Koch.
observations: Three heavy capitals are spaced far apart, one for each founder's surname.
A green cut inside the K is the only colour, a small detail that makes the mark recognisable.

logoResearch.name: Strategy&
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Strategy& is the strategy consulting arm of PwC, formed from Booz & Company in 2014.
observations: A heavy serif sets the name in lowercase, which feels confident but approachable.
The ampersand ending the name hints at partnership and makes the name easy to remember.

logoResearch.name: Simon-Kucher
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Simon-Kucher was founded in Bonn, Germany, in 1985 and is known for pricing strategy.
observations: The founders' surnames are stacked in bold capitals with a cluster of red diamonds.
The strapline "Unlocking better growth" sits under the name in the same red.

logoResearch.name: Deloitte
logoResearch.verifiedFact: William Welch Deloitte opened his first office in London in 1845.
observations: A heavy, rounded sans serif sets the name in black.
The bright green dot after the name is the most recognisable full stop in professional services.

logoResearch.name: PwC
logoResearch.verifiedFact: PwC was formed in 1998 when Price Waterhouse merged with Coopers & Lybrand.
observations: A heavy lowercase serif makes the three letters feel solid and friendly.
Two orange blocks above the letters are a simplified version of the firm's earlier colourful mark.

logoResearch.name: EY
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ernst & Young shortened its name to EY in 2013.
observations: Two heavy capitals sit under a yellow beam that slopes upward.
The beam is a visual hint at progress and makes the short name feel energetic.

logoResearch.name: KPMG
logoResearch.verifiedFact: KPMG was formed in 1987 when Peat Marwick International merged with Klynveld Main Goerdeler.
observations: Italic blue capitals lean forward under a row of four outlined boxes.
Each box sits over one letter, which turns an acronym into a structured mark.

logoResearch.name: Accenture
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Andersen Consulting renamed itself Accenture in 2001.
observations: A simple lowercase wordmark keeps the long name easy to read.
A purple greater-than sign above the t points forward and works as a standalone symbol.

logoResearch.name: Capgemini
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Serge Kampf founded Capgemini in Grenoble, France, in 1967.
observations: The name is set in flowing blue script, unusual for a large consulting firm.
A spade symbol at the end of the name gives the brand a card-game twist.

logoResearch.name: Booz Allen Hamilton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Edwin G. Booz founded the firm in Chicago in 1914.
observations: Heavy, tight black letters shorten the name to Booz Allen.
A small full stop after the name gives it a decisive finish.

logoResearch.name: Alvarez & Marsal
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tony Alvarez and Bryan Marsal founded the firm in New York in 1983.
observations: A tall blue A shaped like a tower is the main symbol.
The letters A, & and M are stacked vertically beside the tower.

logoResearch.name: FTI Consulting
logoResearch.verifiedFact: FTI Consulting was founded in Annapolis, Maryland, in 1982 as Forensic Technologies International.
observations: A navy symbol of columns looks like a classical building.
The initials are spaced far apart over a thin line of small capitals.

logoResearch.name: Arthur D. Little
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Arthur Dehon Little founded the firm in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1886, making it one of the oldest consultancies.
observations: Navy capitals are spaced widely across the full name.
The D in the middle is a blue shape that doubles as a symbol.

logoResearch.name: ZS
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Andris Zoltners and Prabhakant Sinha founded ZS in Evanston, Illinois, in 1983.
observations: A light grey ZS sits next to a mark made of grey and orange stripes.
The striped mark suggests data and layers, which fits a firm focused on analytics.

logoResearch.name: Huron
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Huron was founded in Chicago in 2002 and focuses on healthcare, education and commercial clients.
observations: Very wide, heavy capitals make the short name feel strong and technical.
The logo uses only black, so the shape of the letters does all the work.

logoResearch.name: Guidehouse
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Guidehouse was formed in 2018 from PwC's US public sector business.
observations: A black and green arrow mark points upward like a guide.
A bold sans serif keeps the name clear next to the sharp symbol.

logoResearch.name: West Monroe
logoResearch.verifiedFact: West Monroe was founded in Chicago in 2002.
observations: A ring of navy squares and dots forms an open circle.
The name is set in lowercase, which makes the firm feel friendly and modern.

logoResearch.name: Slalom
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Slalom was founded in Seattle in 2001.
observations: Bright blue lowercase letters are the whole logo.
The rounded, heavy letters feel more like a tech brand than a consulting firm.

logoResearch.name: Mercer
logoResearch.verifiedFact: William Manson Mercer founded the firm in Vancouver in 1945, and it is now part of Marsh McLennan.
observations: A navy symbol looks like a folded ribbon or two linked shapes.
A clean sans serif name in the same navy keeps the logo simple.

logoResearch.name: Capco
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Capco was founded in 1998 and focuses on consulting for financial services.
observations: Tall, condensed black capitals make the short name look bold.
With no symbol and no colour, the logo looks like a headline.

logoResearch.name: Korn Ferry
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Lester Korn and Richard Ferry founded the firm in Los Angeles in 1969.
observations: A green square holds a KF monogram, next to the founders' names in stacked capitals.
The monogram works on its own as a small icon.

listIntro: The boards below show all 27 consulting logos in one consistent format, grouped into strategy firms, the Big Four and large firms, and specialist consultancies.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size, rankings or reputation of the firm.
sectionNames: Big Four and large consulting firms
sectionIntroductions: The top strategy firms use quiet, confident wordmarks, and each one owns a single detail, like BCG's green square, Bain's red or the green inside L.E.K.'s K.
The Big Four and other large firms work in dozens of countries, so their logos are short, bold and built around one colour accent.
Specialist consultancies are freer with symbols, from ZS's striped mark to Guidehouse's arrow and Korn Ferry's KF monogram.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of consulting logos, not a ranking of consulting firms.
Look at how each logo uses type, colour and one detail to signal expertise, scale or a specialism.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a report cover, a slide deck and a recruiting banner.

findings.heading: Initials win
findings.text: BCG, PwC, EY, KPMG, ZS and Capco shorten long names, and Kearney and Strategy& dropped older names entirely. Short names are easier to say, remember and fit on a slide.

findings.heading: One accent beats a symbol
findings.text: Deloitte's green dot, EY's yellow beam, Accenture's purple arrow and BCG's green square are more recognisable than any abstract icon.

findings.heading: Strategy firms stay quiet
findings.text: McKinsey, Bain, Roland Berger and Oliver Wyman use restrained type and little colour to signal discretion and authority.

findings.heading: Tech consultancies look like tech
findings.text: Slalom, West Monroe and Accenture use lowercase, rounded or bright wordmarks that feel closer to software brands.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a consulting logo
checklistItems: Is the firm name easy to read on a report cover, a slide and a phone screen?
Is there one ownable detail, like a colour, dot, beam or monogram?
Does it avoid generic consulting clichés like arrows, bar charts and globes?
Does it fit your clients, from boardrooms to startups or the public sector?
Will it still work in one colour, small in a slide footer or on a recruiting banner?

faq.question: What makes a good consulting logo?
faq.answer: A good consulting logo is easy to read, distinctive and flexible. Most strong examples lead with the firm's name or initials, use one or two restrained colours, and add one ownable detail, such as Deloitte's green dot or EY's yellow beam.

faq.question: Why do so many consulting firms use initials?
faq.answer: Long partnership and merger names are hard to say and fit on slides. Initials like BCG, PwC, EY, KPMG and ZS are shorter, easier to remember and work at small sizes.

faq.question: What colours do consulting firms use?
faq.answer: Navy, black and dark green are the most common because they signal trust and seriousness. Firms that want to stand out add one bright accent, like Deloitte's green, EY's yellow, Accenture's purple or Bain's red.

faq.question: Should a consulting logo have a symbol?
faq.answer: It is optional. Many leading firms use a wordmark only, and the ones with symbols keep them simple, like Capgemini's spade, Guidehouse's arrow or Mercer's ribbon. A simple symbol helps for app icons and social profiles.

faq.question: How much does a consulting logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices range from a few hundred dollars for a template to tens of thousands with a large agency. I design a complete brand identity in one week for a flat $3,000, including the logo, colours, typography and guidelines.
